newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU Commission escapes mad cow censure move for now.
newsitem.headline: EU Commission escapes mad cow censure move for now.

text.p: The European Parliament on Thursday stepped back from censuring the European Commission over its handling of mad cow disease but deputies warned they might do so later.
A parliamentary committee of inquiry rejected an amendment by the Green Group calling for a motion of no-confidence in the Commission, the European Union's executive body.
It was one of 254 amendments to a report attacking the way the Commission had handled the 1996 mad cow crisis, which has undermined the European beef industry, and suggesting reforms.

The mad cow crisis erupted in March 1996 when Britain said that the cattle brain disease, bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE), could be linked to a fatal human equivalent. The EU reacted with a worldwide ban on British beef exports.
The committee's president said European citizens would be angry that the Parliament was not taking stronger action.
"It's very bad for the reputation of the Parliament. We have not used the opportunity offered by the committee of inquiry," German Christian Democrat Reimer Boege told reporters.

Boege, who had expected support from the parliament's two largest political groups -- the Socialists and Christian Democrats -- said that the vote showed that the committee had changed its mind due to domestic political pressure.
"The fight is not over," warned Boege at a news conference after 1 1/2 days of often confused voting on the amendments.
Boege said that the Green Group and Christian Democrats had collected over 100 signatures for a separate censure motion against the Commission if it failed to cooperate with reforms.
Other political groups were also preparing critical motions in readiness for the Parliamentary debate on February 19.
Belgian Socialist Jose Happart, the most radical member of the committee, has already found more than 20 of the required 63 votes in order to present an immediate vote of censure.
Although the report says Britain was mainly responsible for mishandling the crisis, the Parliament has little legal scope to take direct action.

Instead Boege called on the Commission to take British agriculture minister Douglas Hogg to the European Court of Justice for refusing to appear before the inquiry, saying this violated an EU inter-institutional accord of April 1995.
"Clearly something is wrong if the Commission, as guardian of the (EU) treaties, allows that to happen," Boege said.

One of the main demands of the committee is for the creation of a public health protection unit, for both human and animal health, independent of agricultural and industrial interests and controlled by the EU consumer affairs commissioner.
Commission President Jacques Santer told the inquiry in mid-January the Commission planned similar changes.
